final_proof:
Let \(f^{\to}:\mathcal P(S_1)\to\mathcal P(S_2)\) denote the direct-image map, so that \(f^{\to}(A)=f[A]=\{f(x):x\in A\}\). The assertion that \(f^{\to}|_{\tau _1}\) is a surjection from \(\tau _1\) onto \(\tau _2\) means precisely that
\[
\tau _2=\{f[U]:U\in\tau _1\}. \tag{1}
\]

We first prove that \(\tau _2\) is a topology on \(S_2\). Since \(\varnothing,S_1\in\tau _1\), equation (1) gives
\[
\varnothing=f[\varnothing]\in\tau _2,
\qquad
S_2=f[S_1]\in\tau _2,
\]
where the second equality uses the surjectivity of \(f:S_1\to S_2\).

Let \((V_i)_{i\in I}\) be any family of members of \(\tau _2\). By (1), for each \(i\in I\) there is \(U_i\in\tau _1\) such that \(V_i=f[U_i]\). Direct images commute with arbitrary unions, so
\[
\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i
=\bigcup_{i\in I}f[U_i]
=f\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right].
\]
Because \(\tau _1\) is a topology, \(\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau _1\); hence (1) shows that \(\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i\in\tau _2\). The empty-index case gives \(\varnothing\), already shown to lie in \(\tau_2\).

Now suppose \(V,W\in\tau _2\). Choose \(U,Z\in\tau _1\) with \(V=f[U]\) and \(W=f[Z]\). For every map,
\[
f[U\cap Z]\subseteq f[U]\cap f[Z].
\]
The reverse inclusion holds because \(f\) is injective: if \(y=f(u)=f(z)\), where \(u\in U\) and \(z\in Z\), then injectivity gives \(u=z\in U\cap Z\). Therefore
\[
V\cap W=f[U]\cap f[Z]=f[U\cap Z].
\]
Since \(U\cap Z\in\tau _1\), equation (1) yields \(V\cap W\in\tau _2\). By induction, \(\tau_2\) is closed under all finite intersections. Thus \(\tau _2\) is a topology on \(S_2\).

It remains to prove that \(f\) is a homeomorphism. It is already bijective by hypothesis. For any \(V\in\tau _2\), equation (1) supplies \(U\in\tau _1\) such that \(V=f[U]\). Since \(f\) is injective,
\[
f^{-1}[V]=f^{-1}[f[U]]=U\in\tau _1.
\]
Hence \(f:(S_1,\tau _1)\to(S_2,\tau _2)\) is continuous.

Moreover, if \(U\in\tau _1\), then (1) gives \(f[U]\in\tau _2\). For the inverse bijection \(f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\), this says
\[
(f^{-1})^{-1}[U]=f[U]\in\tau _2.
\]
Thus \(f^{-1}\) is continuous. Consequently \(f\) is a homeomorphism, and \((S_2,\tau _2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1\), as claimed.
